sentences.text: The rule in the Bjurholm forest is that you do not look alone.

Nils's grandmother gave it to him at eight, at the second door, on the day she first let him put his eye to one, and she gave it in a way that was not a warning and was not really an instruction either.

Getting out is a separate arrangement, and I am the arrangement." He did not understand and she did not explain, and she stood behind him with a hand on his shoulder while he looked, and after a while she said his name and he stood back.
He asked how long he had been looking.
He asked because his legs had gone and because the light had changed and because there was a mosquito bite on his neck that had not been there.
He had thought it was somewhere under one, and he said so, and his grandmother said, "Yes," and they walked home.

She did this eleven or twelve times over the next two summers and every time she told him the true number afterwards and every time it was between six and twenty minutes, and every time Nils would have sworn on anything that it had been about forty seconds.
He tried counting once, at eleven, on the theory that if he counted seconds he would have a check on it.

He got to about thirty and then found that he had stopped counting at some point he could not identify, and when his grandmother said his name he was on thirty-one and had been at the tree for fourteen minutes.
That is the whole of the phenomenon and Nils has never found a way to make it sound serious.
He knows exactly how it sounds.
It sounds like being absorbed in something — like reading, like a screen, like the thing that happens to every human being who has ever been interested in anything.
He thought that himself, at twelve, and was quite pleased with the thought, and said it to his grandmother.
She said: "Try it in the dark." He went out that November at four in the afternoon with a head torch, to the third door, and he looked in, and his father came and got him at ten past seven.
His father was not pleased and Nils has never blamed him.

It was minus eleven and Nils had been standing still against a tree for three hours in a jacket meant for walking, and his father had gone out on the snowmobile at half six having tried the phone eleven times, and there had been a real and entirely ordinary danger in it that had nothing to do with anything strange.
That is the argument Nils's father has always made about the doors and it is a good one: the interesting thing is not the tree, the interesting thing is a boy standing still in the dark in November.
